title_content.content: Regio- and Stereoselectivities for Alkylation and Boronization of Allenes through Metal−Support Electron Interactions of Single-Atom Catalysts

paragraph_content.content: Shicheng Ren,<sup>∥</sup> Song Lin,<sup>∥</sup> Zeyu Ren, Yang Li, Quanzhou He, Mao-Rui Wang, Fei-Hu Cui, Wen-Hao Li, Hai-Tao Tang,* and Ying-Ming Pan*

ABSTRACT: In synthetic chemistry, controlling the regio- and stereoselectivities, especially nontraditional selectivities, of multicomponent tandem reactions has always been challenging. In organic reactions, single-atom catalysts (SACs) possess fixed coordination structures and adjustable metal−support interactions and frequently generate products possessing well-defined regio- and stereoselectivities. Herein, a silicon carbide (SiC)-supported copper SAC (CuCl @O−SiC) was synthesized using increased copper content and the interaction between the metal support and SiC was regulated through oxygen-based surface modification. Allenes underwent nontraditional β,γ-addition, exclusively generating Z-configured alkylboronization products. These findings revealed the β,γ-selectivity pattern in
allene addition reactions, which advances the application of SACs in chemical catalysis. This work ofers the potential for further developments in selective synthesis.
KEYWORDS: regio- and stereoselectivities addition, allenes, carboboration, silicon carbide support, β,γ-addition, single-atom catalysts

Even for experienced synthetic chemists, rapid, eficient, and cost-efective synthesis of structurally simple multisubstituted olefins remains challenging;<sup>1−4</sup> however, multicomponent synthesis holds tremendous promise for synthesizing multi substituted olefins.<sup>5−7</sup> Nevertheless, the simultaneous integration of diverse substrates within a single step inevitably amplifies the risk of side reactions and exacerbates the complexity of controlling olefinic stereochemistry .<sup>8−13</sup> Because of their distinctive dual perpendicular π-orbital structures and inherent reactivities, allenes have attracted considerable interest in organic synthesis.<sup>14−19</sup> Presently, precisely controlled α,β-additions of allenes through homogeneous copper/ ligand catalytic systems are invaluable for directly fabricating sophisticated multisubstituted olefinic frameworks. 20−23 Among these reactions, the difunctionalization α,β-addition of allenes, at α-sp<sup>2</sup>- and β-sp-hybridized carbon atoms, catalyzed by nucleophilic Cu−B species and predicated on borohydride reaction mechanisms, has emerged as a fervently discussed topic in synthetic chemistry (Figure 1A).<sup>24−27</sup> Despite recent advancements enabling the synthesis of various β,γ-addition products via α,β-addition rearrangements, copper predominantly metallates with α-carbon atoms.<sup>28</sup> Consequently, the multicomponent boron functionalization of allenes, generating branched products via β,γ-addition, remains exceptionally rare.

Navigating these challenges, the generation of internal alkynes from allenes in situ represents a promising approach for atypical selective additions.<sup>29</sup> However, this requires the simultaneous conquering of three pivotal hurdles: First, the conversion from allenes to alkynes must be expedited to suppress unnecessary α,β-addition of allenes to copper−boron intermediates. Second, during rearrangement and addition, the activity of copper catalysts must be sustained to prevent catalyst aggregation and deactivation for the completion of a single catalytic cycle. Finally, to finely tune the reaction’s stereoselectivity, copper catalysts possessing befitting electronic efects must be developed.<sup>30</sup> In such intricate reactions, the catalyst must delicately balance sustained coordination stability and demanding chemo- and stereoselective regulations, which is dificult to achieve using traditional homogeneous metal/ligand catalytic systems (Figure 1B).<sup>31</sup>

In organic synthesis, the development of single-atom catalysts (SACs) is an important advancement in catalyst design.<sup>32−42</sup> Over the past decade, SACs have demonstrated remarkable chemical selectivities and superior catalytic activities because of their unique coordination structures and diverse fundamental characteristics derived from heterogeneous catalytic systems.<sup>43−53</sup> Chemists have sought to deeply understand the structure−catalytic activity dynamics of SACs and the manner in which the carrier regulates the electronic efects of metal catalytically active centers. Consequently, the mechanisms by which SACs coordinate and determine the stereoselectivities of organic reactions have gradually been elucidated.<sup>54</sup> SACs’ distinct inherent coordination abilities make them suitable for satisfying conflicting chemical selectivity requirements, and their robust coordination structures and remarkable catalytic activities prevent catalyst aggregation during tandem reactions, thus substantially improving the catalytic eficiency. By modulating the electronic interplay between the metal and support, SACs may enable the control of the stereoselective addition of Cu−B intermediates, ofering an alternative approach to form β,γ-addition products. (Figure 1C).

paragraph_content.content: To demonstrate the catalyst’s eficacy, a series of experiments were conducted using a homogeneous catalytic system; however, the results were unsatisfactory (Table S1, entries 1−8). To determine the efects of various transition-metal carbides on the selectivity and catalytic activity of alkyne hydroboration, a series of metal-carbide-supported Cu-based SACs was synthesized to evaluate their catalytic activities. The experimental results revealed that during the reaction, diferent metal-carbide supports exhibited distinct selectivities,<sup>55</sup> suggesting that the interaction between the metal support and catalyst plays a crucial role in modulating the regioselectivity of the reaction. Evidently, although both the chromium carbide (CrC) and titanium carbide (TiC) catalysts exhibited low selectivities, their diferent dispersibilities in the solvent hindered suficient contact with the reaction substrates, considerably constraining their catalytic activities (Table S1, entries 9 and 10). After 72 h, the SiC catalyst carrier produced only a relatively low reaction yield of 50% (Table S1, entry 11). To investigate this peculiarity, the catalyst was characterized using inductively coupled plasma−optical emission spectroscopy (ICP−OES). The experimental results revealed that the catalyst’s Cu content was as low as 0.011 wt % because of the high stability of the SiC support, which prevented surface oxidation, and the absence of electrostatic or coordination interactions between the Cu and SiC surface. Therefore, we performed a simple oxygen modification on the surface of SiC to increase the loading of copper atoms. The experimental results revealed that under classical reaction conditions, CuCl @O−SiC possessed the optimal catalytic activity, producing an isolated yield of up to 75% of only the

Studies of the reaction mechanism have revealed that the generation of internal alkyne intermediates from allenes in situ is a crucial first step in controlling the reaction selectivity (Figure S8). Because allenes possess a multitude of potential active sites, extensive computational modeling was conducted to investigate the energy diferences among the various reaction intermediates. This study aims to reveal the specific role of the catalyst in promoting the generation of internal alkynes in situ. When copper is bound to the carbon atoms at the
\beta \mathrm { - }
and γ-positions of allenes, the formed structure
B. Structural diagrams of 1h and 1h'

possessed the most stable energy, facilitating the formation of internal alkynes (Figure S9). Calculations revealed that the energy required for this transformation was 0.59 eV (Figure S10). The plausibility of the proposed theory was experimentally confirmed. The crude product was reacted with allenes for 1 h under standard conditions and then characterized using
^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }

NMR spectroscopy, which displayed diagnostic peaks for the alkyne moiety, including a methyl carbon atomic signal at δ 4.04 and sp-hybridized carbon atomic resonances at δ 85.58 and 79.46 (Figure S11). The signal coincided with the chemical shift of the alkyne intermediate, providing direct evidence of its in situ generation. Furthermore, the binding of copper catalysts to boron plays a key role in achieving high selectivity for internal alkynes, which is also one of the important factors that enables the reaction to proceed smoothly. Because reaction selectivity control depended entirely on the boronization of the Cu-metal catalytic center with alkynes, the Cu−Bpin reactive species produced diferent alkyne intermediates because of the diferent attack directions. Using the basic computational model of Cu SAC, we systematically investigated the energy diferences of various reaction intermediates during copper borylation and in the presence of an iodoalkane, revealing the regulatory role of the catalyst in reaction selectivity. Theoretical calculations revealed that when the copper active center coordinated to the γ-position of the alkyne and reacted with the iodoalkane, the activation energy barrier for the formation of the target product was only 0.91 eV. Conversely, when copper bound to the β-position of the alkyne and reacted with the iodoalkane, a substantially higher activation energy barrier (1.67 eV) hindered target product formation, indicating that the catalyst controlled the reaction selectivity. The theoretical calculations and experimental measurements agreed, confirming that the catalyst system’s exclusively feasible pathway only generated
\beta , \gamma \cdot

-addition products (Figures 3 and S12). In parallel, we investigated the kinetics of the reaction between allenes (1a) and iodohydrocarbons and found that the reaction rate depended on the concentration of either the catalyst and the electrophile (1-iodobutane), indicating that the reaction followed first-order kinetics (Figures S13 and S14). As the reaction rate law was consistent with the mechanism proposed based on the DFT calculation, these results together support the proposed mechanism.

paragraph_content.content: We began by investigating the butylboronization of allenes (1a) with 1-iodobutane and bis(pinacolato)diboron under diferent basic (Table S3) and temperature (Table S4) conditions. The results showed that the optimal conditions were 1a (0.2 mmol), iodohydrocarbons (0.6 mmol), B source (0.26 mmol), CuCl @O−SiC (10 mg), NaO<sup>t</sup>Bu (0.3 mmol), and KO<sup>t</sup>Bu (0.3 mmol) in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) (2 mL) at 45 °C for 7 h.

Under the optimized conditions, we investigated the range of allenes suitable for the reaction. Allene substrates containing electron-donating groups (Figure 4, 2b−2f, 2j), electronabsorbing groups (Figure 4, 2g−2i), naphthalene rings (Figure 4, 2k), and heterocyclic rings (Figure 4, 2l) produced excellent yields of the target products. Moreover, when these substituents were at diferent positions in the benzene ring, they only minimally influenced the reaction yields (Figure 4, 2b−2d). Notably, when internal allenes were used, both the reaction selectivity and yield slightly decreased, which may be related to allenes’ structure (Figure 4, 2m). To further extend the applicability of the catalyst, we chose high-yield 1e as the reaction feedstock and attempted to use iodocarbons (Figure 4, 2n−2t) and diferent B sources (Figure 4, 2u−2v) for the reaction. The results revealed that the catalyst functioned well with these substrates. In addition, we attempted the reaction using a drug molecule as an organic compound fragment and produced compound 2w. Selected examples of unsuccessful attempts are compiled in Table S5.

To systematically evaluate the catalytic eficiency and industrial application potential of this catalyst, we conducted a large-scale reaction, revealing that both the product yield and the selectivity remained virtually unchanged. Similarly, to assess the catalyst reusability, the heterogeneous catalyst was recovered by washing and filtration after each run. Remarkably, the catalyst could be efectively reused for at least six consecutive cycles without losing any of its catalytic eficiency (Figure S15). After the reaction, the catalysts were analyzed using various characterization means, such as HR-TEM (Figure S16A), STEM (Figure S16B), EDS mapping (Figure S16C−F), AC HAADF-STEM (Figure S17), XPS (Figure S18) and EXAFS (Figure S19), revealing that the catalysts morphology, composition, and structure negligibly changed, thereby substantiating the catalysts’ stability under the prevailing reaction conditions.

Overall, the synthesis of complex multisubstituted olefins presents formidable challenges, particularly in accelerating reactions, maintaining catalyst stability, and fine-tuning the reaction stereoselectivity. To overcome these challenges, we synthesized a SiC-supported copper SAC (CuCl @O−SiC) containing increased Cu loadings via oxygen-based surface modification and used the catalyst in the multicomponent boronization of special β,γ-addition-associated branched olefins. These findings should advance research on the synthesis of complex multisubstituted olefins and provide more possibilities for advances and breakthroughs in synthetic chemistry.
